chunks: How a BJT works. The question: How does it work?
A BJT works by letting a small current at the base steer a much larger flow of carriers from the emitter to the collector.
In an NPN, electrons flow from the emitter into a very thin base. Most of them cross the base and get swept into the collector.
A few are lost along the way, and the base current replaces them.
Picture rolling balls across a narrow strip of sticky ground, with a steep downhill slope just past it.
The strip is so narrow that almost every ball makes it across and drops down the slope. Only a few get stuck on the way.
The roller is the emitter, the sticky strip is the base, and the slope is the strong electric field at the collector junction.
The analogy breaks in one place: carriers do not roll in straight lines but wander randomly across the base (diffusion).
A schematic band diagram.

The forward bias lowers the emitter-base barrier so electrons (blue) spill into the base's conduction band; they diffuse across the thin base along the flat part of the diagram and then "fall" down the steep slope of the reverse-biased collector junction.
The drawing is qualitative and not to scale.
Forward-biased junction: a junction pushed in the direction where the barrier is lowered. Minority carrier: electrons in the P-type base are the scarce carrier there.
Recombination: an electron falling into a hole, so both stop being free carriers. Base width: how thin the base is. A thinner base loses fewer carriers.
Current gain ( beta ): collector current divided by base current.
Take an NPN with a gain of about 100. The emitter sends 101 electrons into the base. Because the base is thin, 100 of them cross to the collector.
The cost is about one hole from the base: it is used up by recombination, or it leaks back into the emitter. The base current resupplies that one hole.
So the collector current is about 100 times the base current. That is the whole idea.
"In an NPN the forward-biased base-emitter junction injects electrons from the heavily doped emitter into the thin base.
Most diffuse across before recombining, and the field of the reverse-biased base-collector junction sweeps them into the collector.
